items.prompt: Why can nobody 'catch up' with a fast-moving field?
choices: New releases are mostly written for specialists only
It keeps producing new things at about the same rate
The gap closes only for people who study full time
items.explanation: The stream never pauses for you, so parity is not a reachable state.

items.prompt: What best describes the gap between what the field has produced and what you know?
choices: A permanent, normal feature of working in the field
A temporary debt that clears with enough evenings
A sign that your current learning method needs replacing
items.explanation: The gap is normal and permanent, not a personal failing to eliminate.

items.prompt: Chasing 'caught up' as a goal mainly guarantees what?
choices: A broader skill set than any chosen focus would give
A faster route to genuine depth in each tool
A steady feeling of falling short whatever you do
items.explanation: A target that cannot be reached means the feeling of failure never ends.

items.prompt: A better question than 'have I learned everything new?' is which?
choices: Have I learned the newest tools before my peers did?
Have I learned what moves my work and goals forward?
Have I finished every course I once started?
items.explanation: The first question is always no; the second is answerable.

items.prompt: In the shelf example, the reader covers about 35% of new books a year. What does reading faster do?
choices: It changes the share but leaves the gap open
It closes the gap but costs depth in each book
It makes the shelf shrink after a year or two
items.explanation: Faster reading raises coverage somewhat, yet new books keep arriving, so a gap remains.

items.prompt: Accepting a permanent gap means what for your growth?
choices: You stop growing and rely on past knowledge
You grow, but only on tools your employer pays for
You grow, but measured against your goals instead
items.explanation: It retargets growth; it does not end it.

items.prompt: Which statement reflects the sustainable view of learning?
choices: Every new release is a signal that I am falling behind
The field outproduces any one person, as expected
Rest time is what causes the gap to widen
items.explanation: Expecting the gap removes the guilt each release would otherwise trigger.

items.prompt: Which is a realistic finish line for technical growth?
choices: Learning chosen things that matter to my goals
Knowing every framework released this year
Reaching parity with the field's newest output
items.explanation: Only a chosen, goal-linked target is reachable.

items.prompt: A teammate says, 'Once I finish this backlog of courses I will finally be caught up.' What is the flaw in that plan?
choices: The backlog will not be finished before the courses expire
The field keeps adding items, so the backlog refills as you work
Courses are a weaker way to learn than reading source code in depth
Finishing everything would cost them too many weekends
items.explanation: Parity is not a state the field allows; the flaw is the target, not the effort or the format.
items.reference:
Why there is no finish line
field output: roughly constant per year
your reading: finite hours per year
gap: reopens as fast as it closes
Why: a moving, unending stream cannot be caught up with, so the goal has to be a chosen subset.
items.learnMore:
A permanent gap is normal

The field produces new things at about the same rate whether or not you absorbed last year's output. The useful goal is learning what moves your work, not closing the gap.

Common mistake

Reading each new release as evidence that you personally are behind.
items.reflection: Think of any area (a hobby, a news beat, a genre) that produces more than you can follow. How do you already decide what to skip?

items.prompt: Two engineers see the same product launch. One thinks 'expected, the field always outproduces me'. The other thinks 'I am behind again'. What actually differs?
choices: Their expectation about whether a gap is normal or a failure
Their absolute knowledge, which is higher for the first engineer
Their weekly study hours, which are likely higher for the first
Their employer's training budget, which shapes how they react
items.explanation: The gap is identical; what differs is whether it is read as expected or as failure, which sets the emotional cost.

choices: It reduces the number of hours you need to spend on learning each week
It guarantees that nothing important will be missed later
It works only for people with plenty of unstructured time
It changes the target from 'everything' to 'what moves my goals'
items.explanation: Acceptance retargets growth toward answerable goals; it does not reduce effort or promise completeness.

choices: It shrinks steadily as skills are built through the years
It stays flat, since learning and releases cancel exactly

items.prompt: What triggers curiosity-driven learning?
choices: The announcement of a new release
A teammate mentioning that they enrolled in a course
A real question or a problem in front of you
items.explanation: A held question is the defining trigger.

items.prompt: What triggers anxiety-driven learning?
choices: A question you cannot answer at work
The existence of the new thing itself
A plan you wrote at the start of the year
items.explanation: The launch or headline sets it off, not a question.

items.prompt: Which is typical of anxiety-driven learning?
choices: It feels urgent, with dread if not started
It stays engaging whenever you pause it
It tends to stick, since it is tied to a real use
items.explanation: Urgency and low-grade dread are its signature feeling.

items.prompt: Which is typical of curiosity-driven learning?
choices: Stopping feels like falling further behind
It fades when the launch buzz dies down
You can stop and return later at no cost
items.explanation: A real question waits for you, so pausing costs nothing.

items.prompt: What tends to stick after anxiety-driven study?
choices: Mostly deep, durable understanding
Usually shallow knowledge that fades
Only knowledge of the tool's history
items.explanation: Without a use attached, it often fades once the anxiety passes.

items.prompt: Is anxiety-driven learning always wasted?
choices: No, but it competes for hours with weaker odds
Yes, it teaches nothing real at any point
Yes, unless it happens within a week of the launch
items.explanation: It can teach something; the cost is lower odds of sticking for the same hours.

items.prompt: Two people study the same tool on Saturday. What separates them?
choices: How many hours each of them spent on it
Which of them started earlier
What is driving each one's study
items.explanation: Same behavior, different drivers.

items.prompt: After an engineer drops a new framework and never reopens it, the best guess is what?
choices: Curiosity drove it, now fully satisfied
Anxiety likely drove it, then faded
The framework was too hard for them
items.explanation: Evaporating after the urgency passed is the typical anxiety pattern.

items.prompt: An engineer starts a new database tool the week it ships, and six months later still uses it to fix a slow report. Is launch-week timing evidence of anxiety here?
choices: Yes, starting at the launch shows the launch was the trigger
No, what happened afterward shows a real use was attached
Yes, because curiosity never begins at a launch
No, because only the hours matter, not the timing
items.explanation: Timing alone is weak evidence. Lasting use tied to a real problem points to curiosity.
items.reference:
Same behavior, different driver
trigger: a real question vs the launch itself
feel: engaging vs urgent, low-grade dread
after: retained, revisited vs shallow, fades
Why: the driver, not the hours, predicts what sticks and what it costs.
items.learnMore:
Curiosity versus anxiety

Two people can study the same tool for the same hours. If a question you hold pulls you, it tends to stick; if only the launch pulls you, it tends to fade once the urgency passes.

Common mistake

Judging the driver by launch-week timing alone instead of by what stuck afterward.
items.reflection: Recall something you learned because you needed an answer, and something you learned because everyone was talking about it. Which do you still remember?

items.prompt: Which observation is the best single evidence that a burst of study was anxiety-driven?
choices: The tool was never touched after the urgency passed
It started within days of a major announcement
It took more than ten hours a week for a month
It was done mostly on weekends rather than evenings
items.explanation: What happens after the urgency fades is the clearest tell; timing, volume and scheduling are all consistent with either driver.

The reader retains more, because reading covers more
Neither retains much, because 10 hours is too short
The builder retains more, since a real use is attached
items.explanation: A question and a use tie the knowledge to something durable, so it tends to stick more.

items.prompt: A manager says, 'Stop learning things out of anxiety; only learn out of curiosity.' Why is that advice hard to apply directly?
choices: Anxiety only appears in people who lack real skill
Curiosity cannot be summoned at will on any topic
The driver is not visible from outside, and feels mixed inside
Employers cannot influence what engineers choose to study
items.explanation: The driver often feels blended, so the practical move is a test such as asking whether a real question exists, not a ban.

items.prompt: With 3 hours a week, how many hours is that in a year?
At 30 hours per thing, how many things can 156 hours cover?
Capacity is 5.2 things a year and churn is 15. About what share is covered?
items.explanation: 5.2 / 15 is about 34.7%, so roughly 35%.

items.prompt: If churn rises and your hours stay the same, coverage does what?
choices: Falls, because the same capacity spreads thinner
Rises, since there is a wider range to choose from
Stays the same, set by your hours alone
items.explanation: Same capacity over a bigger total means a smaller share.

items.prompt: If hours per thing doubles, capacity does what?
choices: Doubles, since each thing is richer
Stays the same, set by weekly hours
Halves, since each thing costs more
items.explanation: Capacity is hours divided by cost, so doubling the cost halves it.

items.prompt: At 6 hours a week and 30 hours per thing, about how many things a year?
Why can't you simply add hours until coverage is 100%?
choices: Each added hour must come from rest or life
Capacity is capped by the field's release pace
Churn drops once your hours rise
items.explanation: Extra hours are borrowed from sleep, rest or the rest of life.

items.prompt: In this model, what is 'churn rate'?
choices: Hours a person needs to spend on each new thing to learn it
The share of things you chose to skip
New significant things the field produces per year
items.explanation: It is the field's yearly output of things that plausibly matter.

items.prompt: Assumed numbers: 4 hours a week, 20 hours per thing, 13 new things a year. What share of churn is covered, to the nearest percent?
items.reference:
Assumed numbers: coverage = capacity / churn
3 hrs x 52 weeks = 156 hours a year
156 / 30 hours per thing = 5.2 things
5.2 / 15 new things = about 35%
Why: coverage falls as churn rises, and extra hours raise it only in proportion, so the choice of what to cover matters more.
items.learnMore:
Churn against capacity

Capacity per year is hours per week times 52, divided by hours per thing. Coverage is that capacity divided by yearly churn, capped at 100%. The demo lets you drag all three inputs.

Common mistake

Treating the numbers as universal facts instead of assumed values to reason with.
items.reflection: Estimate your own hours and the cost per new thing. Which one assumption would change the answer most?

items.prompt: A new tool category doubles yearly churn from 15 to 30 while nothing else changes. What happens to coverage at 3 hours and 30 hours per thing?
choices: It halves, from about 35% to about 17%
It stays about 35%, since hours are unchanged
It drops to zero, since capacity is exceeded
It falls only slightly, since capacity adapts
items.explanation: Capacity stays 5.2; 5.2 / 30 = 17.3%, half the earlier 34.7%.

items.prompt: Which change raises coverage the most, with 3 hours, 30 hours per thing, 15 churn as the baseline?
choices: Adding 1 hour a week, which raises yearly capacity by about 1.7 things
Ignoring 3 of the 15 things, which cuts churn to 12
Studying on the weekend rather than on weeknights
Halving the cost per thing by learning only to working level
items.explanation: Halving cost doubles capacity to 10.4 (69%). One extra hour gives about 6.9 (46%), ignoring 3 things gives about 43%, and timing changes nothing.

items.prompt: The coverage chart shows 100% at 5 new things a year and 52% at 10. What is the best reading?
choices: Coverage falls by half whenever churn rises by another 5 things a year

The model breaks down below 10 new things a year
items.explanation: Capacity of 5.2 covers 5 fully (capped); at 10 it is 5.2 / 10 = 52%. The drop is a ratio, not a fixed step.

items.prompt: How many questions make up the learning filter?
choices: Seven
Three
Eight
items.explanation: Relevance, durability and genuine interest.

items.prompt: Which is one of the filter's questions?
choices: Is it relevant to my current work or goals?
Is it popular on social media right now?
Is it free to try for the first month?
items.explanation: Relevance to work or goals is the first question.

items.prompt: What does 'durability' ask?
choices: Whether the tool is hard to break
Whether the docs are well maintained
Whether it will matter in about two years
items.explanation: It asks whether it will still matter, or be replaced before it compounds.

items.prompt: What does 'genuine interest' ask?
choices: Whether colleagues find it interesting
Whether a real question pulls you toward it
Whether it appears in job postings
items.explanation: Interest apart from relevance and durability: a real question pulling you.

items.prompt: A tool fails all three questions. What does the filter suggest?
choices: Skip it for now, since it is likely anxiety
Learn it right away, just to stay safe and ahead
Wait for a colleague to learn it first
items.explanation: Three nos mean the buzz is generating the pull.

items.prompt: When should the filter be applied?
choices: After finishing the first tutorial
When the course ends
Before committing any hours
items.explanation: Deciding before starting is what saves the hours.

items.prompt: A skipped tool becomes relevant after you change teams. What now?
choices: Nothing, a skip is permanent
Run the filter again, since a no was for that moment
Learn it, as skipping was a mistake
items.explanation: A no is a verdict on the current moment, not a lifetime ban.

items.prompt: Does a yes to just one question justify learning something?
choices: Often yes, one real reason can be enough
Never, all three must be yes
Only when the yes is for durability
items.explanation: One genuine yes is often reason enough.

items.prompt: A tool fails relevance but you are quietly fascinated by how it works, and it is likely to last. What does the filter say?
choices: Skip it, since relevance is a required pass
Learn it, since two of three questions are yes
Skip it, since fascination usually fades once you try it
Learn it only after your team adopts it
items.explanation: A yes to any one question can be enough, and here interest and durability both are yes.
items.reference:
Three questions, asked before starting
Relevance: does it touch current work or a real goal?
Durability: will it matter in about two years?
Interest: is a real question pulling you?
Why: a yes to any one is often enough; no to all three means the pull is probably anxiety.
items.learnMore:
The filter

Ask the three questions before starting, not three hours into a tutorial. A no is a verdict on the current moment, so a skipped tool can pass later if your work changes.

Common mistake

Running the filter after hours are already sunk, which only produces guilt.
items.reflection: Pick one thing you are tempted to learn right now. What would your answers to the three questions be?

items.prompt: After three hours into a tutorial for a trending tool, an engineer runs the filter and answers no, no, no. What is the main problem?
choices: Three hours are sunk, so the filter now breeds guilt
The filter gives the wrong answer for trending tools
The engineer should have asked a colleague instead
Three hours is too short to judge durability fairly
items.explanation: The filter saves hours only if run first. Run afterward, it can only generate guilt about time already spent.

items.prompt: Skipping a tool in March, an engineer's project in October needs it daily. Which statement is correct?
choices: The March skip was a mistake that should be undone
The filter failed and should be dropped from now on
Skips should be treated as permanent to save effort
The March verdict held for then; rerunning now gives a yes
items.explanation: A no covers the current moment. Changed work changes the relevance answer, which is not a failure of the filter.

items.explanation: Interest asks whether a real question pulls you. Buzz is the anxiety trigger, not a question.

items.prompt: In year 2 the engineer had no filter. What did they do with each launch?
choices: Skipped it until it proved durable
Asked their manager whether to learn it
Treated it as urgent to learn right away
items.explanation: Without a filter every launch felt urgent.

items.prompt: Roughly how many hours a week did the year-2 peak reach (assumed)?
choices: About 25
About 15
About 30
items.explanation: The unit's assumed peak is about 15 hours a week.

items.prompt: What was the outcome of the year-2 pattern?
choices: Shallow exposure to nearly everything
Deep skill in one framework
A promotion on the strength of breadth
items.explanation: Broad and shallow, with little real competence.

items.prompt: What did the manager notice?
choices: Rising deployment speed
A new interest in management
Falling code-review quality
items.explanation: Review quality slipped, prompting the question.

items.prompt: In year 4, what happened before any hours were committed?
choices: A weekend trial of each tool
Each new thing went through the filter
A vote among the teammates
items.explanation: The filter was applied first.

items.prompt: Which cloud tool got deep learning in year 4?
choices: Kubernetes
Service mesh tool A
A trending serverless framework
items.explanation: It was relevant, durable and interesting, so it passed.

items.prompt: Why were the service mesh tools skipped?
choices: They were too expensive to evaluate
They were banned by the team
They had no relevance to current work and unclear winners
items.explanation: No multi-service traffic problem, no clear winner, no interest.

items.prompt: Roughly how many hours a week did year 4 take (assumed)?
choices: About 15
About 5
About 20
items.explanation: Roughly 5 hours a week.

items.prompt: Year 2 had roughly 780 hours a year of learning and still little competence. What best explains that?
choices: The field was too complex for any one engineer to learn well
Hours were split across starts and restarts, none taken far
The engineer lacked talent for the new frameworks
Weekend study is less effective than weeknight study
items.explanation: Hours were plentiful on paper, but divided over abandoned starts, so none reached competence.
items.reference:
Year 2 versus year 4, same field
Y2: no filter, ~15 hrs/wk, little competence
Y4: filter first, ~5 hrs/wk, real Kubernetes depth
change: decision before hours, not hours
Why: the field's churn did not slow; the engineer's choice of what to start did.
items.learnMore:
What changed between year 2 and year 4

Not the churn and not the free time. The engineer decided what to start before starting it, so fewer hours went to restarts and more to one thing taken past competence.

Common mistake

Concluding that fewer hours alone caused the improvement.
items.reflection: Think of a time you took on too many things at once. What would a filter have removed first?

items.prompt: Which change best explains year 4's better outcome with fewer hours?

The field slowed its release pace during that year
The engineer took a break from learning that year
The team took over the engineer's learning work
items.explanation: Churn did not slow. Deciding before starting concentrated the hours on one thing.

The hours were a symptom; what to start was the lever
items.explanation: A fixed number of hours is not the lesson. The same 5 hours scattered across everything would repeat year 2.

items.prompt: In the year-4 table, a trending serverless framework scored 'mild interest, only trending'. Why is Skip still right?
choices: Mild interest never outweighs any other factor

The engineer had already learned Kubernetes by then
items.explanation: It failed two questions, and the interest was buzz, not a held question. A yes needs a real one.
items.reference:
Year 2 versus year 4, same field
Y2: no filter, ~15 hrs/wk, little competence
Y4: filter first, ~5 hrs/wk, real Kubernetes depth
change: decision before hours, not hours
Why: the field's churn did not slow; the engineer's choice of what to start did.
items.learnMore:
What changed between year 2 and year 4

Not the churn and not the free time. The engineer decided what to start before starting it, so fewer hours went to restarts and more to one thing taken past competence.

Common mistake

Concluding that fewer hours alone caused the improvement.
